articles.title: Sanctuary for All
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: The following remarks were delivered by ROC DSA Co-Chair Gregory Lebens-Higgins at the Rochester Contemporary Art Center’s (RoCo) “Route of Refusal: A Public Art Walk” on Saturday, October 3, held as part of the national 2026 Fall of Freedom weekend . The event mixed creative art and expression with community and activism, including poetry that invoked words censored by the Trump regime, and collective music-making. RoCo’s current featured exhibit, “ Sanctuary: Borders & Belonging in 2026 ,” is a mixed-media presentation on dichotomies of sanctuary and isolation. “Projects in the exhibition amplify immigrant voices, document criminalization and detention, examine border politics and architecture, and give impacted people space to share diverse immigration stories.” The exhibit runs until November 14. ROC DSA is planning a group outing. DSA is creating a world of sanctuary for all from the predations of capitalism. A world of safety, a world free from exploitation, a world of access to the means for a dignified life. We know our immigrant neighbors are among the most vulnerable. That race is a tool used to justify and enforce their hyperexploitation. Those who speak up, those who try to organize, are the first targeted for detention and deportation. Because when the working class does act in solidarity, when we do call out with unified voice, we present a challenge to the unearned power of our rulers. Let us create a sanctuary that is not defined by borders, but by inclusion and acceptance. A sanctuary not limited to the privileged few. The Protect Our Neighbors campaign is calling on the Monroe County Legislature to declare our county a place of sanctuary for our immigrant neighbors by providing assurance that local resources will not be used for federal immigration enforcement. The county must also use its financial leverage by divesting from companies involved in the construction and operation of immigrant detention centers. Join the call by emailing your legislator at bit.ly/pon_email . We’ll also be hosting a canvass kick-off on Oct. 10 @ 11:30am in Maplewood Park, collecting petition signatures throughout our community. Help us to build a network of sanctuary, organizing our momentum locally, nationally, and worldwide. Participate in ICE watch, ensuring their activities are not done in the dark. Support mutual aid, so vulnerable communities are not unnecessarily exposed. The only way we respond effectively is together. The post Sanctuary for All first appeared on Rochester Red Star .

articles.title: Getting Fired from Mother Jones Made Michael Moore
articles.author: Bhaskar Sunkara
articles.content: Before Paul Berman became a liberal hawk, he was a New Left veteran who edited a book called Quotations from the Anarchists . In 1986, his long-standing anxiety about the authoritarian left may have produced a casualty: Michael Moore’s magazine career. Moore had edited Mother Jones for five months when he tried to kill the second installment of Berman’s two-part commissioned dispatch on Nicaragua. Berman did identify the Contras as US-financed, traced their leadership to Anastasio Somoza Debayle’s National Guard, and acknowledged the “blood on their hands.” But his overarching concern was Sandinista Leninism: their restrictions on political competition and refusal to share power. Moore was unmoved. “The article was flatly wrong and the worst kind of patronizing bullshit,” he said. “You would scarcely know from it that the United States had been at war with Nicaragua for the last five years.” With Washington funding a counterrevolutionary army and the civil war’s outcome very much in doubt, Moore worried about the impact the article could have. President Ronald Reagan, he complained, could wave it around and say, “See, even Mother Jones agrees with me.” He’d wanted Alexander Cockburn writing on Nicaragua instead of “neo-nudnik Paul Berman.” He also might have suspected that his erstwhile anarchist writer, though denouncing the “true psychopaths” leading them, had some latent sympathies for rank-and-file Contras. Reporting from Nicaragua for the New Yorker a decade later, Berman would write that the group’s popularity in the countryside “was overwhelming,” and that their claim to be “the largest guerrilla movement in the modern history of Latin America was entirely correct.” By then, he and journalist Joan Kruckewitt had traveled through northern Nicaragua tracking down members of the Contra unit that killed Ben Linder, the young American engineer ambushed while building a dam for a hydroelectric project. They found a commando whom official reports placed at the ambush — a devout, teetotaling Assembly of God preacher known as Williams. Williams denied personally taking part in the attack, despite his signature on the reports and his detailed recollection of the events. Berman nevertheless found the Contra veteran strikingly similar to the victim: “fervently idealistic,” “likable,” and “admirable.” “It was just that one was living and the other was dead.” It was Sandinista land seizures, price controls, conscription, and Cuban advisers, not just American money and propaganda, that Berman blamed for driving Nicaragua’s peasantry into the Contra ranks in the first place. Back in 1986, Mother Jones chairman Adam Hochschild, who bankrolled much of the magazine’s budget himself, was unmoved by Moore’s objections. He called to say, “I am exercising my prerogative as chairman of the board of directors and ordering you to run this piece.” Publishing the Berman piece, in Hochschild’s thinking, would counteract any suspicion that the magazine was carrying water for the Sandinistas. Moore, still smarting, had decided to run it after all, planning to include an editorial rejoinder alongside it. Before he could, Hochschild rang again, out of the blue, and fired him: “You’ve created a crisis situation.” He offered Moore two months’ pay and help getting his things back to Flint, Michigan, on the condition that Moore sign a statement describing the split as a “no-fault separation.” Moore refused. Afterward, Hochschild would deny that the Berman fight had been the real cause at all, citing vague “personnel problems” to Cockburn that he wouldn’t specify. Moore was adamant that he was ousted because he “did not want to print lies about Nicaragua,” and his supporters speculated that Hochschild had wanted a working-class editor’s image without a working-class editor’s independence. But it all worked out in the end. Moore sued for wrongful termination and received $58,000, which he put into Roger & Me , his celebrated 1989 documentary about General Motors plant closures in his hometown of Flint. While Berman’s article did not defeat Leninism, the spat his reporting inspired helped Moore build an audience of millions without having to kowtow to a publisher. It was an impressive win for political pluralism on the Left. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Reckoning With the Failures of Tech Worker Organizing
articles.author: Alex N. Press
articles.content: In early 2022, a group of Twitter employees were quietly trying to unionize the company. They called themselves the “Starlings” after the birds whose synchronized flight patterns offer one another safety and warmth. The workers mapped out their coworkers and assessed their pro- or antiunion sentiments, held one-on-one conversations, and tried to stay off of management’s radar while they built toward a majority. Then Elon Musk bought Twitter. Half the workforce disappeared in the first round of layoffs , with cuts falling heavily on trust and safety and other teams where the union had organizers. Twitter’s employee directory went offline, and the offices temporarily closed. Against Tech Oligarchy: Worker Resistance in the World’s Most Powerful Industry , a new book by organizers JS Tan and Clarissa Redwine, begins with the Twitter organizing drive. Redwine, who had helped unionize Kickstarter , joined the Twitter campaign in early 2022; Tan, coming off a successful graduate worker drive at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, joined a few months later. They were still organizing when Musk took over, suddenly making much of the work they had done impossible to continue. “With half the company gone and internal organizations completely decimated,” write Tan and Redwine, “the most basic steps of the Recognition Playbook — from mapping the workplace to conducting one-on-one conversations — had suddenly become exceptionally hard.” The union drive died. The authors had arrived at the Twitter campaign after years of organizing in and around the tech industry. Tan was a software engineer at Microsoft when, in 2019, he traveled to Kazakhstan to show Chevron employees how Microsoft’s machine-learning tools could be used in an oil field. While he was there, Amazon employees published an open letter demanding that their employer stop building custom tools for oil and gas companies. Tan was doing that work for Microsoft. When he returned home, he anonymously wrote about the trip. “Oil Is the New Data” described Microsoft helping Chevron increase oil production and Chevron employees asking about using technology to monitor workers. “We knew that they simply wanted a way to discipline their low-wage Kazakhstani workforce,” Tan wrote. “We knew they wanted a way to squeeze as much work as they could from each worker.” In Against Tech Oligarchy , he and Redwine supply the part that did not appear in the article: “JS was interrogated and eventually pushed out” for publishing it. Redwine’s route into the movement ran through Kickstarter, where a union drive had stalled at just over 50 percent support by the summer of 2019. (Most union drives build to supermajority support before calling for a vote, since support for the union inevitably flags in the face of antiunion measures by the boss.) She and two other visible organizers were fired ; Kickstarter denied that the firings had anything to do with the union. The firings had the opposite effect from the one organizers feared. “Instead of killing the campaign,” Tan and Redwine write, “the firings reignited it.” People who had been sitting on the fence showed up to a union meeting. In February 2020, Kickstarter workers voted 46–37 to unionize. Tan and Redwine went on to help other tech workers pursue the same basic strategy: organize a majority, win recognition, bargain a contract. But Against Tech Oligarchy looks back at that turn with considerable doubt. Wages, benefits, and job security increasingly took precedence over fights about what the companies were building in the first place. And the drive to build overwhelming support before taking on management gave workers fewer chances to learn through conflict, leaving them woefully unprepared for the scorched-earth response that came once they challenged their employers. Tan and Redwine are reconsidering advice they once gave workers themselves. Much of the book is an effort to understand why all the organizing in tech over the past decade has left workers with so little lasting power. The Tech Worker Movement Union drives like Kickstarter and Twitter grew out of a tech worker movement whose ambitions initially extended well beyond winning better conditions at work. Tan and Redwine were both members of the Tech Workers Coalition , which argued for an expansive definition of who counted as a tech worker, including contractors, cafeteria workers, content moderators, and office workers alongside engineers and designers. For the authors, that definition is essential: without a common struggle between engineers and “the cafeteria staff who fed them, or the content moderators who kept the internet clean,” the authors write, “any challenge to tech capital would remain partial and fragile.” At Google, the first big fight came over Project Maven , a Pentagon program using artificial intelligence to analyze drone footage. The contract drew a revolt inside the company. Thousands of employees signed a letter opposing the work, and several quit. Google eventually said it would let the contract expire. Later that year, some twenty thousand Google employees walked out over the company’s handling of sexual harassment. Management initially made an odd show of embracing the walkout. Organizer Claire Stapleton’s manager gave her a pair of Dr Martens to commemorate it. But before long, Stapleton and fellow organizer Meredith Whittaker said the company retaliated against them, and both eventually left. The fight over dissent continued with Timnit Gebru, the coleader of Google’s Ethical AI team. After a dispute over a paper in December 2020, Gebru said Google fired her; Google claimed it had accepted her resignation. Her departure prompted months of protest inside the company. By then, tech workers had also discovered the limits of publicity as a source of leverage. Tan and Redwine found that leverage from press attention “peaked sharply within the first forty-eight hours and quickly vanished from public consciousness as attention shifted to the next news cycle.” Public campaigns also required recognizable spokespeople, giving management “clear targets for retaliation.” Thousands of people might sign a letter or join a walkout without having built the relationships needed to sustain a fight. The actions, the authors write, were often driven by a handful of people and could function “quite effectively on shallow relationships and temporary participation.” The turn toward unions came out of those experiences. The earlier campaigns could bring thousands of workers into action without building an organization capable of surviving retaliation or the end of the news cycle. The standard organizing path recommended by the international unions that tech workers began affiliating with — what Tan and Redwine call the “Recognition Playbook” — offered a different approach: build a representative organizing committee, develop majority support, win voluntary union recognition or a National Labor Relations Board election, and bargain a first contract. That slower work promised to leave workers with something durable when a particular fight was over. By 2021, a year after Kickstarter workers won their union, there were fifteen newly minted tech unions. “Whereas ethical and social issues, such as curbing emissions or canceling military contracts, animated the previous era of the movement,” Tan and Redwine write, “the new playbook called for a focus on bread-and-butter issues”: pay, health care, job security. In 2018, roughly 80 percent of documented collective actions in tech concerned issues beyond the workplace. By 2022, fewer than one in five did. Tan and Redwine eventually became staff organizers for the United Electrical, Radio and Machine Workers of America (UE), which the Starlings affiliated with as their campaign grew. At Twitter, they put this approach into practice, helping the committee work quietly toward the goal of a supermajority. “As we grew closer to the formal labor establishment,” they write, “our own sense of what was possible narrowed.” Their “fervor for ambitious social and political demands gave way to a focus on bread-and-butter issues” that could more readily be won in a contract. They came to believe that the strategy had done something more damaging too: it deferred conflict until workers had accumulated enough support to win. But “experiencing conflict is an essential part of union building”: delaying it deprives workers of the moments that teach them “what tactics are effective against the boss and how the boss might respond to a challenge.” Later in the book, New York Times Tech Guild organizer John Cruickshank distills the problem: “Action builds capacity for action.” The Recognition Playbook narrowed more than the movement’s tactics. Earlier fights had often been about the work itself. Workers at Google did not want to help the Pentagon analyze drone footage; Amazon workers objected to their company helping oil and gas companies extract more fossil fuels. A union contract gave organizers something concrete to fight for, but it also tended to put wages, benefits, and job security at the center of the campaign. Whether workers should be building a particular technology in the first place was harder to fit into that model. The challenge is how to combine the ambitions of that earlier movement with an organization capable of making them costly for an employer to ignore. Some of the book’s strongest analysis concerns how changes in the industry itself have altered workers’ leverage. For years, tech companies competed fiercely for skilled workers. One former Facebook employee recalled Meta “just hoarding us like Pokémon cards.” A worker unhappy with a job could often get more money by going somewhere else. That became a less reliable option once companies started laying people off . More jobs were being done by contractors too: by 2023, they accounted for nearly one in five tech jobs, three times the share two years earlier. And for workers on visas, getting fired or laid off carried another risk: eventually, they could lose the right to stay in the country. Fighting had become more expensive. Learning How to Strike What happened at Twitter after Musk’s takeover made the problem of worker leverage unusually stark. He eventually eliminated close to 80 percent of Twitter’s workforce, producing what Tan and Redwine call “a sudden withdrawal of labor on a massive scale.” But the company continued to function: “The code still executed, the servers still hummed, and the ads kept generating revenue.” The New York Times Tech Guild offered another test. More than six hundred workers unionized in 2022 and spent more than two years bargaining a first contract. In November 2024, they walked out just before the presidential election, when the paper expected enormous traffic. But in the weeks before the strike, management told employees to “gold-plate” the platform, and workers helped prepare the site to withstand their absence. Eight days later, the strike was over and the site had kept running. Some of the obstacles here are hardly particular to tech. High turnover, fragmented workplaces, management delay, drawn-out legal processes, and workers’ reluctance to take risks for gains they may never see are familiar well beyond tech companies. The nature of the work is different. In much of the industry, Tan and Redwine write, “the whole point of tech work is to automate production and build products, platforms, and services able to run without workers present. . . . When labor stops, code keeps running.” They argue that “the way in which workers can strike effectively has yet to be discovered.” AI may further weaken some tech workers’ leverage. It can transfer control “from workers to algorithmic systems owned by employers,” taking workers’ “tacit knowledge that had previously resisted codification” and embedding it in the tools themselves. Managers have long sought to take knowledge that resides with workers, break it into reproducible parts, and put greater control over the labor process in their own hands. AI gives that process a peculiar form in tech, where some of the workers whose knowledge can be captured by the technology are also building it. AI is also changing the industry’s physical geography. Tech was never immaterial: its software and platforms have always depended on mines, chip fabs, warehouses, electrical grids, and enormous workforces. But the platform companies could expand into new markets without building much new fixed infrastructure in each place they entered. Building AI requires data centers, chips, huge amounts of electricity and water, and a great deal of capital. Those facilities, Tan and Redwine write, depend on “state-issued permits, access to municipal water, favorable electricity pricing, and local zoning approval.” Tech is becoming “anchored in national territory and contingent on political approval.” The build-out may also create new sources of worker power. Data centers cannot be moved at the speed of software. They need electricity and water from the surrounding area, and workers have to build it and keep it running. AI may make some tech workers easier to replace while making the industry more reliant on others. Building all of this also brings tech companies into much closer contact with the state. The AI boom has made companies that once styled themselves as largely independent of government increasingly reliant on energy policy, permits, infrastructure, and other forms of public support. In January 2025, Donald Trump appeared at the White House with Sam Altman, Larry Ellison, and Masayoshi Son to announce Stargate , a planned AI infrastructure investment of as much as $500 billion. Tan and Redwine’s “tech oligarchy” is an economic elite increasingly acting together politically, with corporate power deeply entangled with state power. Workers were discovering themselves as workers at roughly the same time that their bosses were discovering themselves as a class. By the end of Against Tech Oligarchy , Tan and Redwine have come a long way from the Recognition Playbook they once promoted. They want to recover some of the ambitions of the movement’s beginnings, when workers asked why they were building military technology, software for immigration enforcement, or tools they believed would worsen climate change. The book’s final section is called “An Invitation,” and that describes its spirit: an attempt to leave other workers a record of the path they took, including the wrong turns, so they might get further the next time. Nor can tech workers rein in the class that controls the industry on their own. AI’s physical expansion makes that especially clear. The industry increasingly connects programmers to the workers who build data centers, manufacture chips, maintain servers, supply electricity, and construct the infrastructure on which the tech economy has always depended. If tech’s power now runs more decidedly through infrastructure and the state, figuring out how tech workers can exercise power at work is one part of the problem. Figuring out how that power connects to the power of everyone else with a hand on the same system is another. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Trump’s Politically Driven Deportations Are Quietly Rising
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: Donald Trump’s approval on immigration is so deathly low, and his ongoing deportation raids so unpopular even in red states, that you’d be forgiven for thinking his administration has pumped the brakes on the issue. Instead the White House is advancing a radical agenda that is increasingly targeted not at criminals or even law-abiding undocumented people but at legal immigrants. Pro-Palestinian activist and green card holder Mahmoud Khalil may have staved off his politically motivated deportation, but the Trump administration is only expanding its targeting of permanent residents. It just got the go-ahead to deport an Israel critic and leader of the largest mosque in Wisconsin, Salah Sarsour, based on decades-old convictions in Israel — namely, that he threw a rocks at members of the Israeli military while living in the West Bank and that he tried to own weapons, actions the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) calls terrorist activity. A Trump-appointed district judge had previously ruled that he had presented a “substantial” case showing the administration was going after him over his pro-Palestinian speech. Mohsen Mahdawi, the fourteen-year-long permanent resident who became an early flash point in the Trump administration’s free speech crackdown after he was arrested at his citizenship interview, remains at risk of deportation. This past June, a judge ordered that Mahdawi, who alongside Khalil cofounded Columbia University’s Palestinian Student Union, be deported to Jordan. Unlike with Sarsour, the administration has not even bothered to accuse Mahdawi of a crime. His deportation is based purely on punishing him for his constitutionally protected speech, claiming that his campus pro-Palestinian activism would have “potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences.” These are just two of the most politically motivated cases in a growing trend : that of green card holders being detained and having deportation proceedings started against them, often based on years-old convictions or other flimsy grounds . Dozens of other green card holders were slated for deportation by a new DHS unit whose express purpose is revetting their permanent residency. It’s not just green card holders. Ya’akub Vijandre, a Muslim photojournalist originally from the Philippines, had his Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) status revoked and was arrested and detained over social media posts the government claims were “endorsing or espousing terroristic activity.” Given that Vijandre’s posts — some of which the federal government hasn’t even produced but simply alleges he made — were allegedly about the kind of due process violations that are typical in writing about “war on terror” excesses, it raises the question of whether simply criticizing government policy while being an immigrant qualifies as a crime in Trump’s America. The administration’s hostility extends even to US citizens. Making good on its threat to ramp up the stripping of citizenship, denaturalization efforts have hit a record high , with 105 suits filed in the first seven months of the year. While the government has released information about some of those successful cases highlighting very real and odious crimes to justify denaturalization, little is known about most of these cases and their underlying basis, making it hard to know if at least some of these cases are similarly politically motivated as the administration’s targeting of permanent residents like Khalil and Mahdawi. But there’s still one more milestone the administration has hit with its turn to targeting legal migrants. Last month saw the very first successful deportation case for the thirty-year-old Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC), a special tribunal that can deport noncitizens based on secret evidence that the accused is not allowed to see or challenge. Using this system, forty-seven-year-old green card holder Nazira Haji Zada was sent to Afghanistan and banned permanently from the United States, with the government never even charging her in the criminal justice system. As attorney Eric Lee, who serves on former Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipient Vijandre’s legal team, wrote for Just Security , the case brings up many of the concerns that have been raised about the ATRC, including in the way the court itself and its expansive authority can be used to coerce noncitizens into signing away their rights. (Zada ultimately agreed to be deported and conceded that she was a terrorist when faced with the ATRC.) Since she was challenged based on secret evidence, it’s impossible to evaluate the merits of the case against her. But given how broadly the administration has defined criminal or terrorist activity in other deporation cases against noncitizens — including simply pro-Palestinian activism and social media posts — and given how it internally defines terrorists as effectively anyone who criticizes or protests against its own policies, mostly on the Left, you have to wonder: Whatever Zada was or wasn’t guilty of, was hers simply the case that will open the door to the Trump administration using the ATRC to deport its noncitizen political opponents for speech and other First Amendment–protected activity it doesn’t like? The Trump administration suffered a major political defeat on its deportation efforts in Minneapolis at the start of this year and, as a result, made a public show of moderating. But what has followed since is a quiet but fundamental reshaping of the American immigration system, which is being slowly transformed into a weapon for advancing the president’s and his party’s political goals — namely, to destroy the pro-Palestinian movement and the Left more broadly — and one where noncitizens, no matter their exact status, are viewed as having little more rights than tourists. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: The West Is Only Helping Putin Consolidate Support
articles.author: Leonid Ragozin
articles.content: At the “We Shall Not Be Moved” event in New York on September 21, Senator Bernie Sanders delivered a programmatic speech that attacked the United States’ staggering trillion-dollar war budget. He described the war industry draining the life out of society as a global and not just American problem. This is why, he said, progressives should oppose Donald Trump’s war in Iran, Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and the United Arab Emirates’ proxy war in Sudan. This is also why “we must rally and work with grassroots activists in Russia to put an end to Putin’s disastrous war in Ukraine,” Sanders asserted. Had he been addressing an audience of the said Russian activists, his comment would have come across as uninformed and tone-deaf. Hardly any of them are physically in Russia to begin with — and hopes of returning any time soon are dim. The war has allowed Vladimir Putin to wipe out the opposition and civil society at large, forcing the vast majority of people involved to leave the country for fear of spending the rest of their lives in torture prisons. Sanders might be envisaging a grassroots antiwar movement like the one he participated in during America’s war in Vietnam. But he didn’t face anything remotely similar to the eight-year prison sentence — handed down the day after his speech — upon Mikhail Antonovich from Tyumen in Western Siberia, who simply left some paid likes (generating tiny automatic donations) under Telegram posts by pro-Ukrainian commentators. However, the main problem is bigger. There are fundamentals at the heart of this conflict that Russian opposition activists can’t possibly change, because they’d need to change the West itself. They all ultimately boil down to that same trillion-dollar industry Sanders is fighting against and its corrupting influence on democracy, media, and policy expertise in Western countries. The West in its current rudderless, jingoistic, and trigger-happy state is Putin’s best insurance against any uprising at home. Statements about defeating or dismembering Russia delivered by senior Western politicians like the current EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas achieve little beyond solidifying Putin’s support. So do Ukrainian drones attacking Moscow and St Petersburg. Russians of all political leanings can see what the United States and its main proxy are doing to Iran and Gaza. The last thing they want is to follow the Ukrainians and swap their still relatively comfortable life for someone else’s delusional geopolitical project that ignores their interests or goes squarely against them. When, back in October 2022, members of Congress’s Progressive Caucus produced a letter urging President Joe Biden to seek a diplomatic solution to the war in Ukraine, Sanders said that he disagreed with the call and then praised its eventual retraction. Fall 2022 was an ideal period for Ukraine to negotiate peace and avert at least another four years of catastrophic devastation. Ukraine had just liberated swathes of the Kherson and Kharkiv regions, while the Russian army seemed inept and unprepared to face the power of Ukrainian resilience. That period is sometimes called “Milley’s window” after the Joint Chiefs of Staff chairman, General Mark Milley, who claimed that there was a window of opportunity to achieve peace because, despite its success, Ukraine wasn’t able to defeat Russia militarily. But the Biden administration was up in arms against the proposal because it believed in what Milley considered impossible: Russia’s military defeat. The following year showed that Milley was right: Ukraine’s 2023 counteroffensive, planned together with the Americans and the Brits, turned out to be a massive failure. Meanwhile Russia rebuilt its forces, resuming the offensive and making a giant leap forward in terms of modernization and battlefield innovation, crucially outpacing the West in drone warfare. So how come Sanders turned out to be more bent on Russia’s defeat than America’s most senior general? Perhaps he’d bought into the discourse promoted by the same trillion-dollar war industry he is fighting against, backed by its pet think tanks and media. Spare the Oligarchs, Bash the Activists At least Sanders takes a different line than the full-time warmongers on the issue of the Russian opposition. The warmongering community in the West tends to see it as a nuisance: it makes it harder to cast all Russians as Putin’s accomplices as best, or as alien monsters (derided as “orcs”) dead set on destroying Western civilization. The industry devotes its efforts to hardening polarization and erasing the zone of cohesion. Along with Ukrainian war skeptics like President Volodymyr Zelensky’s former press secretary Iuliia Mendel, anti-Putin Russians are one such zone. This explains why they sometimes appear to be bashed more readily by government-linked pro-Ukrainian and pro-NATO online mobs like the “North Atlantic Fella Organization” (or NAFO) than the Kremlin. A couple of run-of-the-mill stories in September illustrate Western attitudes to antiwar Russians and real-life practices in dealing with them. Last week, the EU decided to lift sanctions from two Russian oligarchs, Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman. The decision sparked outrage among Russian opposition figures. “It turns out that for Europe, it doesn’t really matter whether you support the war or not, whether you are friends with Putin or oppose him. In the end, what seems to matter far more is how much money you have in your bank accounts,” wrote Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of Aleksey Navalny, who died in prison when he returned to Russian after surviving a near-lethal poisoning. “Shame on you EU,” wrote Vladimir Kara-Murza, himself a survivor of a poisoning attack. There are two reasons for their outrage. The first regards these oligarchs themselves, at least Usmanov (Fridman is a more nuanced case). Opposition activists believe that Usmanov actively assisted the Kremlin in exerting control over independent media and social networks by purchasing politically sensitive media assets, such as Kommersant , a major business newspaper, and VKontakte, the Russian equivalent of Facebook. Its founder, Pavel Durov, was coerced into selling this asset, upon which he fled Russia and founded Telegram. Both Usmanov and Fridman have never publicly opposed Putin’s regime and war in Ukraine. Neither are they known for funding the opposition. Meanwhile, most Russian antiwar exiles feel that they are being punished more severely than any of Putin’s oligarchs, given their incomparably lower financial means and virtually absent legal support. They are subject to a whole of array of sanctions and discriminatory measures introduced by the United States, the EU, and its individual member states against Russian nationals, which appear to be driven more by xenophobia and revenge than any war-related rationale. Asked to comment on Navalnaya’s reaction, EU’s official representative Arianna Podesta lashed out at Russians at large: “It is up to the Russian people themselves whether they will have a government that supports this war or not. Therefore, if Russian citizens are feeling the consequences of this war first-hand, they have the opportunity to take action against it within their own country.” “I can’t find polite words to respond to it,” Kara-Murza tweeted in response. Senator Sanders doubtless believes Russian “grassroots activists” must be their country’s true patriots, who want a better life for the Russian people after the fall of Putin’s dictatorship. But this is definitely not the kind of Russian activists the West seeks to support in practice. On September 3, the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) decided to throw out 879 cases against the Russian state filed by Russian citizens, prominently including the same anti-Putin activists of which Sanders spoke. Russia was kicked out of the Council of Europe, the ECHR umbrella organization, in 2022, so the court decided that even complaints filed prior to this date aren’t worth considering. Fried Onions Early this year, the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe established a delegation of the Russian opposition known as the Platform for Dialogue with Russian Democratic Forces. Some of its members voiced disagreement with the decision and drafted an appeal against it. But the majority of the delegation, including figures like chess champion Garry Kasparov, didn’t support the move. To explain why, it’s worth looking into how the platform was created. Its formation was mired in scandals from the outset. For starters, it was presided over by the former Estonian intelligence chief Eerik-Niiles Kross, whose views on Russians at large were reflected in a recent tweet that shows a xenophobic advertisement from an Estonian meat producer that extolls the virtues of barbecuing “onions” (a derogatory Estonian-language expression for Russians, Kross helpfully explained). When the platform was being created, Kross made a point of excluding the only opposition force that has a real following in Russia, Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK). Most members were supplied by an unofficial network associated with fugitive oligarch Leonid Nevzlin, currently an Israeli businessman and a shareholder of the daily Haaretz . Figures associated with Nevzlin’s network take a radical pro-Ukrainian stance, for instance supporting the neo-Nazi Russian Volunteer Corps that fights on Ukraine’s side under the auspices of Ukrainian military intelligence. Members of the unit run the neo-Nazi platform Wotan Jugend that circulated the Russian translation of the manifesto penned by Christchurch massacre’s perpetrator. But the problem associated with Nevzlin-backed personalities runs deeper. In 2024, the FBK published an investigation that accused Nevzlin of organizing a violent attack in Lithuanian capital Vilnius on Leonid Volkov — a senior FBK personality and longtime Navalny ally. Prior to its expulsion from Russia, FBK conducted groundbreaking corruption investigations targeting Putin and his entourage. Despite this, Kross lashed out at FBK after the publication of this investigation for duplicating the work of police in democratic countries. Alas, the Polish prosecutor’s office brought charges against Nevzlin’s legal associate who confirmed the oligarch’s involvement to investigators, although he later retracted his testimony in court. Hardly groundbreaking, these stories simply add to an already giant pile of questions to the West regarding the war in Ukraine. There are doubtless more pressing issues. What is the deeper wisdom of turning a blind eye toward Ukraine’s brutal mobilization (known as “busification”) even as videos from passersby daily offer heart-wrenching evidence of what this means for those press-ganged into the army? How is squeezing the Russian language from public use in Odesa — a city that produced a unique Jewish-influenced Russian-language culture that spans every type of art — helpful for the Ukrainian cause? What is the point in pretending that former skinheads play no role in Ukraine while they are commanding whole armies with a clearly far-right ideological slant? Why should Ukraine keep bleeding in the cause of expanding NATO, when it could have exited the war on much better conditions under the Minsk Accords or the settlement framework drafted by Ukraine and Russia in Istanbul in spring 2022? Or, indeed, during Milley’s window, when Senator Sanders chose to side with “fight-Russia-till-the-last-Ukrainian” types of the Lindsay Graham variety? The question that looms largest is whether, by helping Ukraine, the West is promoting its declared values, like democracy and human rights — or simply pursuing an imperialist geopolitical project in which members of the Russian opposition, but more importantly Ukrainians, must be satisfied with the role of useful idiots and cannon fodder while their countries are being destroyed. Does the West really see Putin and his oligarchs as its deadly enemies — or rather as partners in the lucrative and mutually beneficial business of fomenting wars? This is the question US progressives need to answer before encouraging the Russian opposition to storm the Kremlin. articles.title: How United Airlines became a link in Israel’s weapons supply chain
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: United Airlines has been sending military hardware to Israel on passenger flights, right under your feet. A new report from the People’s Embargo for Palestine, the Palestinian Youth Movement, and others documents 2,761 shipments of military cargo to Israeli weapons manufacturers and military institutions, including Elbit Systems, Lockheed Martin Israel, Nevatim Airbase, and the Israeli Ministry of Defense. Belal Elsiesy, organizer with the PYM and the People’s Arms Embargo, joins Zoe Alexandra to break down the findings. With cargo including F-35 bomb release units used to drop 2,000-pound bombs on Gaza, Merkava tank sights, and “hunter-killer” machine gunner sights destined for Elbit, Elsiesy argues civilian airports are a critical point of intervention. He also discusses what’s behind Elbit’s US rebrand as 26 Defense, how campaigns against Maersk and FedEx have targeted the weak links in Israel’s weapons supply chain, and why the airline’s silence on the #NoWeaponsOnUnited campaign is a good reason to act now.
